results.result: The authors developed a new method called Aggregate Mutation Spectrum Distance (AMSD) to detect mutator alleles by comparing aggregate mutation spectra between haplotype groups. The method minimizes multiple testing burdens and mitigates sparsity challenges in de novo mutation datasets. Simulations show AMSD has ~90% power to detect a mutator allele that increases C>A mutation rate by 20% with 100 haplotypes averaging 500 mutations each, but <20% power for C>G mutators of identical effect size. AMSD performs similarly to QTL mapping overall but shows superior power when mutation counts vary substantially across haplotypes or when mutator allele frequencies are <50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C44-C45, C50-C53, and C55-C57 collectively describe the AMSD method and its performance characteristics. The simulation results (C51-C52, C55-C57) provide quantitative evidence for the method's power under various conditions, with appropriate statistical thresholds (p=0.05). The claims are internally consistent and supported by simulation data shown in supplementary figures.

results.result: AMSD was applied to 117 BXDs with 65,552 de novo germline mutations and successfully re-identified the previously discovered mutator locus on chromosome 4 at marker rs27509845 (118.28 Mbp, 90% CI: 114.79-118.75 Mbp). This locus overlaps 21 DNA repair genes, with only Mutyh containing nonsynonymous differences between parental strains. Mutyh encodes a protein involved in base-excision repair of 8-oxoguanine, and C>A mutation fractions are nearly 50% higher in BXDs with D genotypes at this locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C68 describe the successful validation of AMSD by re-identifying a known mutator locus. The specific genomic coordinates, confidence intervals, and mutation rate differences are provided with appropriate statistical support. This serves as a positive control demonstrating that AMSD can detect known mutator alleles.

results.result: Using AMSD on BXDs with D genotypes at the chromosome 4 locus, a novel mutator locus was identified on chromosome 6 at marker rs46276051 (111.27 Mbp, 90% CI: 95.01-114.02 Mbp). This signal was specific to BXDs with D genotypes at chromosome 4, as no significant loci were found in BXDs with B genotypes at that position. The chromosome 6 region contains 64 protein-coding genes, including 4 DNA repair genes (Fancd2, Ogg1, Setmar, Rad18), with Ogg1 and Setmar harboring nonsynonymous differences between parental strains. Traditional QTL mapping failed to detect this locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C79 describe the discovery of a novel mutator locus using AMSD. The conditional analysis strategy (stratifying by chromosome 4 genotypes) is well-justified and the specificity of the signal (C72-C73) provides strong evidence for epistasis. The failure of QTL mapping to detect this locus (C75) demonstrates AMSD's superior sensitivity in this context.

results.result: C>A mutations were significantly enriched on BXD haplotypes with D genotypes at the chromosome 6 locus (χ²=85.36, p=2.48e-20). C>A mutation fractions were significantly higher in BXDs with D alleles at both mutator loci compared to either locus alone. After controlling for inbreeding duration, BXDs with D alleles at both loci were predicted to have 238.9 C>A mutations (95% CI: 231.4-246.4) after 100 generations, approximately 20% more than those with D alleles only at chromosome 4 (199.0 mutations, 95% CI: 193.3-204.7). Importantly, D alleles at chromosome 6 alone did not elevate C>A mutation fractions in BXDs with B alleles at chromosome 4.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 provide strong statistical evidence for the mutator effect and its conditional nature. The chi-square test (C85), comparison of mutation fractions (C86), and regression model predictions (C89-C90) with confidence intervals all support the epistatic interaction. The critical observation that chromosome 6 D alleles have no effect without chromosome 4 D alleles (C87) is essential for establishing epistasis.

results.result: Mutation signature analysis revealed that SBS1, SBS5, and SBS30 signatures were active in nearly all BXDs regardless of genotypes at the mutator loci. However, the SBS18 signature (dominated by C>A mutations and reflecting unrepaired ROS damage) was almost exclusively active in mice with D alleles at chromosome 4, with highest activity in mice with D alleles at both loci. SBS18 activity was lowest in mice with D alleles only at chromosome 6, demonstrating that D alleles at this locus are insufficient to cause a mutator phenotype alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 provide independent validation of the epistatic interaction through mutation signature analysis. The pattern of SBS18 activity across genotype combinations is consistent with the epistatic model and provides mechanistic insight linking the mutator phenotype to oxidative DNA damage. The observation that chromosome 6 D alleles alone show minimal SBS18 activity (C95-C96) strongly supports the conditional nature of this mutator.

results.result: Statistical modeling demonstrated that a model including an interaction term between genotypes at the two mutator loci fits the data significantly better than a model with only additive effects (p=7.92e-7), indicating that the combined effects of D genotypes at both loci exceeded the sum of marginal effects at either locus alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 provide formal statistical evidence for epistasis through model comparison. The highly significant p-value (7.92e-7) from the likelihood ratio test strongly supports non-additive genetic effects. The methods section describes appropriate Poisson regression models accounting for inbreeding duration and sequencing coverage.

results.result: In the Mouse Genomes Project (MGP) strains, only DBA/1J and DBA/2J possess D genotypes at both mutator loci. A model with an interaction term did not fit the MGP data significantly better than an additive model (p=0.806), failing to confirm the epistasis signal, possibly due to the smaller number of MGP strains with mutation data.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 describe an attempt to validate the epistasis in an independent dataset that yielded negative results. While the authors speculate this may be due to limited sample size (C101), the lack of replication raises questions about the generalizability of the epistatic interaction. However, this does not invalidate the BXD findings, as the MGP analysis is underpowered with only 2 strains having the relevant genotype combination.

results.result: Analysis of wild mouse populations revealed that the Ogg1 D allele segregates at 25.9% frequency in M. musculus domesticus (from which C57BL/6J and DBA/2J derive most of their genomes) and is fixed in M. musculus musculus, M. musculus castaneus, and M. spretus. The Setmar p.Ser273Arg D allele was present at 37% frequency in M. musculus domesticus, while the Setmar p.Leu103Phe and Mbd4 p.Asp129Asn D alleles were absent from all wild populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 provide important evolutionary context for the candidate mutator alleles. The data show that some candidate variants (Ogg1, Setmar p.Ser273Arg) segregate in wild populations, while others (Setmar p.Leu103Phe, Mbd4 p.Asp129Asn) appear to be laboratory-specific. This information is relevant for assessing which variants are most likely causal and whether the mutator phenotype might occur in natural populations.

results.result: The authors argue that Ogg1 is the most plausible candidate gene for the chromosome 6 mutator locus based on several lines of evidence: (1) Ogg1 is a glycosylase that excises 8-oxoG lesions and is a member of the same BER pathway as Mutyh, (2) Ogg1 contains a nonsynonymous fixed difference (p.Thr95Ala) between parental strains, and (3) Ogg1 appears to be regulated by cis-eQTLs across multiple tissues in the BXD cohort. Other candidate genes (Setmar, Fancd2, Rad18, Mbd4) are considered less likely based on functional considerations and lack of appropriate genetic variation or expression differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C127 present a reasonable argument for Ogg1 as the causal gene, but the evidence is circumstantial. The authors acknowledge they have not conclusively fine-mapped to a causal variant (C121). While Ogg1's role in the same BER pathway as Mutyh is compelling, the p.Thr95Ala variant is not predicted to be deleterious by SIFT and occurs at a poorly conserved position (C153-C154). The eQTL evidence (C127) is suggestive but comes from non-germline tissues. Additional functional validation would be needed to definitively establish causality.

results.result: The Ogg1 p.Thr95Ala variant is not predicted to be deleterious by SIFT and occurs at a nucleotide that is not well conserved across mammalian species. The authors speculate that this variant may not be highly deleterious on its own and might only exert detectable effects when Mutyh function is also impaired. Alternatively, D alleles at Ogg1 may lead to very subtle increases in C>A mutation rates that the study is underpowered to detect independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C156 acknowledge important limitations in the evidence for Ogg1 p.Thr95Ala as the causal variant. The lack of predicted deleteriousness and poor conservation (C153-C154) are inconsistent with a strong functional effect. The speculation about conditional effects (C155) is reasonable given the epistasis but remains unproven. The alternative explanation of insufficient power (C156) cannot be ruled out. These uncertainties highlight the need for functional validation.

results.result: Strong cis-eQTLs for Ogg1 expression were observed across multiple tissues in the BXDs, with D genotypes consistently associated with decreased Ogg1 expression. Combined with evidence that an intronic mobile element insertion in Mutyh may cause decreased Mutyh expression at the chromosome 4 locus, the authors propose that both mutator loci may increase C>A mutation rates by lowering expression of DNA repair genes in the same BER network. This suggests the effect of the chromosome 6 locus may be conditional on expression of the Mutyh mutator, indicating complex genetic interactions can underlie germline mutator phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C165 present an attractive mechanistic hypothesis linking both mutator loci through reduced expression of BER pathway genes. The eQTL evidence for Ogg1 (C160-C161) is solid, and the parallel with Mutyh (C162) is compelling. However, the eQTL data come from non-germline tissues, limiting direct applicability to the germline mutator phenotype. The proposed mechanism (C163-C165) remains speculative and would require validation through germline expression studies and functional experiments.

results.result: The Mbd4 p.Asp129Asn variant resides within the Mbd4 methyl-CpG binding domain, occurs at a well-conserved position, and is predicted to be deleterious by SIFT. A homologous human variant (p.Asp142Gly) is predicted to be deleterious/probably damaging. However, loss-of-function mutations in Mbd4 are typically associated with C>T mutagenesis at CpG sites rather than C>A mutations, and no excess C>T mutations were detected in BXDs with D alleles at the chromosome 6 locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C173 present conflicting evidence regarding Mbd4 as a candidate gene. The variant characteristics (C166-C170) suggest potential functional impact, but the mismatch between expected (C>T) and observed (C>A) mutation spectrum (C171-C173) argues against Mbd4 as the causal gene. The authors acknowledge this puzzle but do not resolve it. Mbd4 also lies outside the 90% confidence interval, further reducing its likelihood as the causal gene.

results.result: AMSD successfully identified a mutator allele on chromosome 6 that escaped detection by QTL mapping. While simulations show AMSD and QTL mapping have similar power overall, AMSD outperformed QTL mapping in the BXD dataset, likely because AMSD compares aggregate mutation spectra rather than weighting individual samples equally. This property is advantageous when haplotypes carry highly variable numbers of mutations, as in the BXDs where older lines have accumulated orders of magnitude more mutations than younger lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C192 provide a clear comparison of AMSD and QTL mapping performance. The empirical demonstration that AMSD detected a locus missed by QTL mapping (C185, C187) is compelling. The simulation results (C186, C188) and mechanistic explanation (C191-C192) for AMSD's superior performance in the BXD context are well-supported. The variable mutation accumulation across BXD breeding epochs (C189-C190) provides a plausible explanation for why AMSD's aggregation approach was advantageous.

results.result: While popular QTL mapping methods like R/qtl2 use linear models that enable flexible inclusion of covariates and kinship matrices, the methods to account for inter-sample relatedness in AMSD are not as flexible as those in QTL mapping software.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C197 acknowledge a limitation of the AMSD method compared to established QTL mapping approaches. This is an honest assessment of the method's current capabilities. The authors do describe methods to account for relatedness in the Materials and methods section, but acknowledge these are less flexible than QTL mapping implementations.

results.result: The study demonstrates epistasis between germline mutator alleles in a whole-animal context for the first time. The chromosome 6 mutator locus amplifies the C>A germline mutator phenotype in BXDs, but only in the presence of the chromosome 4 mutator allele near Mutyh. BXDs with mutator alleles at both loci have greater numbers of C>A mutations than those with mutator alleles at either locus alone. This observation suggests that mild DNA repair deficiencies can compound one another as mutator alleles affect redundant systems maintaining germline integrity. While epistasis between mutator alleles has been documented in yeast and human cell lines, this represents the first demonstration in a whole-animal model.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C46-C49, and C108-C113 collectively establish the novel finding of epistasis between germline mutator alleles in a whole animal. The evidence is strong: conditional AMSD analysis (C8, C46), mutation count data (C9, C47, C110), statistical modeling (C97-C98), and mutation signature analysis (C91-C96) all converge on the same conclusion. The claim of novelty (C113) appears justified based on the cited literature (C111-C112). The mechanistic interpretation about redundant DNA repair systems (C48-C49) is reasonable though speculative.

results.result: The authors developed a new method called 'aggregate mutation spectrum distance' (AMSD) to detect alleles associated with mutation spectrum variation. AMSD minimizes multiple testing burdens and mitigates sparsity challenges in de novo mutation datasets by leveraging the fact that mutator alleles leave distinct impressions on mutation spectra. Simulation studies demonstrate that AMSD has approximately 90% power to detect C>A mutators with 20% effect size given 100 haplotypes with 500 mutations each, and outperforms QTL mapping under certain conditions including variable mutation counts and low allele frequencies.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the AMSD method as innovative and well-validated. Reviewer 1 states the method 'is innovative and outperforms traditional QTL mapping under most conditions, as demonstrated by extensive simulations.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the analysis is rigorous and well motivated' and that the authors 'test the statistical properties of their method using simulated data and permutation tests.' Reviewer 3 judges 'the theoretical premise of the AMSD method is judged to be both strong and innovative.'

results.result: Using AMSD on 117 BXDs with 65,552 de novo mutations, the authors rediscovered a previously identified locus on chromosome 4 (peak at 118.28 Mbp) significantly associated with mutation spectrum variation. This locus overlaps 21 DNA repair genes, with only Mutyh containing nonsynonymous differences between parental strains. Mutyh encodes a protein involved in base-excision repair of 8-oxoguanine and prevents C>A mutations, with C>A mutation fractions nearly 50% higher in BXDs with D genotypes at this locus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as validation of the AMSD method. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'first successfully re-identify a known mutator locus in this population on chr4' as 'proof-of-principle.' The editor notes this demonstrates the method can identify mutator loci. No reviewer questions the rediscovery of the chromosome 4 locus or its association with Mutyh.

results.result: A novel locus on chromosome 6 (peak at 111.27 Mbp, 90% CI: 95.01-114.02 Mbp) was significantly associated with mutation spectrum variation specifically in BXDs with D genotypes at the chromosome 4 locus. The region contains 64 protein-coding genes, including 4 DNA repair genes (Fancd2, Ogg1, Setmar, Rad18), with Ogg1 and Setmar harboring nonsynonymous differences between parental strains. This signal was specific to mice with D alleles at chromosome 4, as no new loci were detected in mice with B alleles. QTL scans for individual mutation types did not produce genome-wide significant signals.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this as a major discovery. The editor states the study 'identifies a new "mutator" locus in a population of inbred mouse strains.' Reviewer 1 notes 'convincing evidence for the major findings, including the new candidate mutator locus.' Reviewer 3 describes this as an 'exciting discovery' that 'adds to the catalog of known mutator alleles.' The conditional nature of the effect is explicitly acknowledged by reviewers.

results.result: The chromosome 6 locus exhibits epistatic interaction with the chromosome 4 mutator locus. BXDs with D alleles at both loci have significantly higher C>A mutation rates than those with D alleles at either locus alone, while D alleles at chromosome 6 alone show no significant effect. After 100 generations, mice with D alleles at both loci were predicted to have 238.9 C>A mutations versus 199.0 in mice with only chromosome 4 D alleles (20% increase). A statistical model with an interaction term fits significantly better than an additive model (p=7.92e-7), indicating synergistic effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously affirm the epistasis finding. The editor states the authors 'demonstrate that this new mutator locus interacts epistatically with a previously identified mutator allele.' Reviewer 1 notes 'more rigorous statistical testing, the authors show convincingly synergistic epistatic effects between the mutator alleles at the two loci.' Reviewer 2 states 'The evidence presented for an epistatic interaction is convincing.' Reviewer 3 calls this an 'exciting discovery' that 'reveals key aspects of mutator biology.'

results.result: Mutation signature analysis revealed that SBS1, SBS5, and SBS30 signatures were active in nearly all BXDs regardless of genotype. However, the SBS18 signature (dominated by C>A mutations reflecting unrepaired ROS damage) was almost exclusively active in mice with D alleles at chromosome 4, with highest activity in mice with D alleles at both loci. SBS18 activity was lowest in mice with D alleles at chromosome 6 alone, demonstrating that D alleles at this locus are insufficient to cause a mutator phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss the mutation signature analysis, but they accept the overall epistatic interaction findings which these data support. The signature analysis provides mechanistic insight into the C>A mutator phenotype that reviewers implicitly accept through their endorsement of the epistasis conclusions. No reviewer questions the signature analysis or its interpretation.

results.result: The authors argue that Ogg1 is the most plausible candidate gene for the chromosome 6 locus based on multiple lines of evidence: it is a member of the same BER pathway as Mutyh, contains a nonsynonymous difference (p.Thr95Ala) between parental strains, and shows strong cis-eQTLs with D genotypes associated with decreased Ogg1 expression in multiple tissues. Ogg1 and Mutyh have distinct roles in the BER response to oxidative DNA damage, with Ogg1 recognizing and removing 8-oxoG lesions paired with cytosine, while Mutyh excises mispaired adenine opposite 8-oxoG.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly notes 'the causal gene(s) and allele(s) within this locus remain uncertain.' While reviewers accept the identification of the chromosome 6 locus, they do not explicitly endorse Ogg1 as the causal gene. The authors themselves acknowledge uncertainty, stating they 'have not conclusively fine-mapped the chromosome 6 mutator locus to a causal variant.' The mechanistic model involving Ogg1 is plausible but unproven.

results.result: The p.Thr95Ala Ogg1 variant is not predicted to be deleterious by SIFT and occurs at a poorly conserved nucleotide. The authors speculate this variant may not be highly deleterious on its own and might only exert detectable effects when Mutyh function is also impaired, or alternatively that D alleles at Ogg1 lead to very subtle effects that the study is underpowered to detect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss the functional predictions for the Ogg1 variant. The authors present this as speculation about why the variant might show conditional effects. The uncertainty about the variant's deleteriousness contributes to the overall uncertainty about Ogg1 being the causal gene, which the editor explicitly acknowledges.

results.result: Setmar is another candidate gene at the chromosome 6 locus, with two missense variants between parental strains, one predicted deleterious. However, the murine Setmar ortholog lacks the Mariner transposase domain present in primates, and primate SETMAR is involved in NHEJ repair not expected to affect C>A mutation rates. No significant cis-eQTLs were observed for Setmar, making it an unlikely candidate for the epistatic interaction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss Setmar, but they accept the authors' overall assessment that the causal gene remains uncertain. The authors' reasoning for excluding Setmar as a strong candidate is logical and based on functional considerations. No reviewer challenges this assessment.

results.result: Mbd4 is an additional candidate gene involved in BER that lies just outside the 90% confidence interval but within 10 Mbp of the peak. The p.Asp129Asn variant in Mbd4 resides in a conserved protein domain and is predicted deleterious by SIFT. However, Mbd4 deficiency is typically associated with C>T rather than C>A mutations, and no excess C>T mutations were detected in BXDs with D alleles at chromosome 6.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss Mbd4 as a candidate. The authors present evidence both for (predicted deleteriousness, conservation) and against (wrong mutation spectrum, location outside confidence interval) Mbd4 as the causal gene. This contributes to the overall uncertainty about gene identification that the editor acknowledges.

results.result: Long-read genome assemblies revealed that the chromosome 4 Mutyh mutator phenotype may be caused by a ~5 kbp mobile element insertion in the first intron associated with reduced Mutyh expression. No compelling evidence for structural variants or mobile elements was found at the chromosome 6 locus. The presence of strong cis-eQTLs for Ogg1 suggests the chromosome 6 mutator phenotype may be mediated by regulatory rather than protein-altering variants. The authors speculate that both loci may increase C>A mutations by lowering expression of BER genes in the same network.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss the structural variant analysis or the regulatory hypothesis. The authors present this as speculation ('raise the exciting possibility') about mechanism. While the eQTL data are presented as factual, the interpretation that regulatory variants mediate the phenotype remains speculative and is not explicitly endorsed by reviewers.

results.result: The authors propose that mild DNA repair deficiencies can compound one another as mutator alleles affect redundant genome maintenance systems. They speculate about potential mechanisms involving Mbd4's role in apoptosis: mice with deficient 8-oxoG repair due to Mutyh mutations might accumulate ROS damage, but functional Mbd4 could trigger apoptosis to mitigate effects; however, mice with reduced activity of both genes may have impaired apoptosis responses, leading to higher ROS-mediated damage and elevated C>A mutations. This represents the first documentation of epistatic interactions between mutator alleles in a whole-animal context.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors suggest some plausible potential mechanisms for how this interaction might arise' but cautions that 'given the higher degree of complexity of the proposed model it needs to be treated with greater caution, perhaps until replicated in a separate dataset or demonstrated in follow-up experiments.' The mechanistic speculation is acknowledged as plausible but unproven. The novelty claim about whole-animal epistasis is not explicitly challenged by reviewers.

results.result: AMSD successfully identified the chromosome 6 mutator locus that escaped detection by QTL mapping. While simulations show AMSD and QTL mapping have similar power under many conditions, AMSD outperforms QTL mapping when mutation counts vary substantially across haplotypes (as in the BXDs where oldest lines have orders of magnitude more mutations than youngest lines) and when mutator allele frequencies are below 50%. AMSD's advantage comes from comparing aggregate mutation spectra rather than weighting each sample equally.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm AMSD's superior performance in the BXD context. Reviewer 1 states AMSD 'outperforms traditional QTL mapping under most conditions, as demonstrated by extensive simulations.' Reviewer 2 notes the method 'has greater power to detect genetic factors with a certain magnitude of effect' in the analyzed situation. The comparative analysis is accepted as demonstrating AMSD's advantages under specific conditions.

results.result: The AMSD method has limitations compared to QTL mapping: methods to account for inter-sample relatedness are less flexible than in QTL mapping software, and AMSD currently assumes individuals harbor one of two possible genotypes at each marker without accounting for heterozygous genotypes. As a result, AMSD is currently applicable only to resources like BXD RILs where individuals have been inbred sufficiently that all genotypes are effectively homozygous, and will require modification before application to outbred, sexually reproducing populations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'the main limitation of the approach is that it is difficult to see how it might be applied beyond the context of mutation accumulation experiments using recombinant inbred lines' due to requirements for accumulated mutations linked to mutator alleles. Reviewer 3 states 'there are some limitations to the AMSD method' but judges 'the authors present a balanced summary of the strengths and weaknesses of their method.' The limitations are acknowledged and accepted.

results.result: Attempts to confirm the epistatic interaction in the Mouse Genomes Project (MGP) strains were unsuccessful, as a model with an interaction term did not fit significantly better than an additive model (p=0.806). The authors speculate this may be due to the smaller number of MGP strains with mutation data, as only two MGP strains (DBA/1J and DBA/2J) possess D genotypes at both loci.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss the MGP validation attempt. The authors acknowledge the inability to confirm epistasis in this independent dataset, which introduces some uncertainty about the generalizability of the finding, though reviewers do not raise this as a major concern. The lack of replication is noted but attributed to sample size limitations.

results.result: The discovery of a second BXD mutator allele demonstrates the power of RILs for dissecting genetic architecture of mutation rates. The authors propose that AMSD could be useful for future mutator discovery in other model organisms with RIL populations as sequencing costs decrease, and potentially in large human trio datasets where rare mutator alleles may eventually be represented in sufficient numbers. Mutation spectrum analyses may have greater power than overall rate analyses to detect genes underlying heritable mutation rate variation, even for genes with modest effects.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'the new method has the potential to be applicable to a variety of experimental systems and natural populations.' Reviewer 1 notes the method 'reveals new biological insights.' Reviewer 2 states the method 'could have wide application and impact on our understanding of this fundamental biological process.' Reviewer 3 judges 'the methodology could be extended to other species and populations to enable discovery of additional mutator alleles.' Reviewers affirm the broader applicability and significance.

comparisons.comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly support the AMSD method and its validation through simulations (C6, C44-C45, C50-C57). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence and statistical thresholds, while peer reviewers highlight the method's innovation and rigorous testing. Complete agreement on method validity.

Both evaluations support the successful re-identification of the known chromosome 4 mutator locus (C58-C68). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of genomic coordinates and statistical support, while peer reviewers accept this as proof-of-principle validation. Strong concordance on this positive control result.

Both strongly support the discovery of the novel chromosome 6 mutator locus (C69-C79, C108). OpenEval emphasizes the conditional analysis strategy and epistasis evidence, while peer reviewers describe this as an 'exciting discovery' and major finding. Complete agreement on the significance and validity of this discovery.

Both strongly support the epistatic interaction between chromosome 4 and 6 loci (C85-C90, C97-C98, plus C8-C10, C46-C47, C110 from peer review). OpenEval details statistical evidence while peer reviewers unanimously affirm 'convincing' evidence for synergistic epistasis. Complete concordance on this central finding.

Both support the mutation signature analysis showing SBS18 activity patterns consistent with epistasis (C91-C96). OpenEval explicitly discusses mechanistic insights linking to oxidative DNA damage, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this through endorsement of overall epistasis findings. Agreement on supporting evidence.

OpenEval R6 addresses formal statistical testing of epistasis via likelihood ratio test (C97-C98), which peer reviewers in R4 accept as part of the 'rigorous statistical testing' demonstrating epistasis. Both support the statistical evidence, though peer review groups this with broader epistasis claims.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the MGP validation attempt (C99-C101). OpenEval notes the negative result raises questions about generalizability but doesn't invalidate BXD findings due to limited power. Peer reviewers don't explicitly discuss this but don't raise it as a major concern. Aligned uncertainty.

OpenEval R8 discusses evolutionary context of candidate variants in wild populations (C102-C107). No corresponding peer review evaluation found that specifically addresses this evolutionary analysis, though it informs gene identification discussions elsewhere.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the identification of Ogg1 as the causal gene (C121-C127 plus related claims). OpenEval notes circumstantial evidence and lack of predicted deleteriousness, while the editor explicitly states 'the causal gene(s) and allele(s) within this locus remain uncertain.' Strong concordance on uncertainty.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the functional predictions for Ogg1 p.Thr95Ala (C153-C156). OpenEval details limitations including lack of deleteriousness prediction and poor conservation. Peer reviewers don't explicitly discuss but this contributes to overall uncertainty about Ogg1 acknowledged by editor. Aligned uncertainty.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the mechanistic hypothesis involving reduced BER pathway gene expression (C160-C165 plus related claims in R6). OpenEval notes eQTL evidence is from non-germline tissues and mechanism remains speculative. Peer reviewers accept this as part of overall uncertainty about causal genes. Agreement on speculative nature.

OpenEval R11 discusses regulatory hypothesis and structural variants (overlapping with C162-C163), while peer R10 addresses broader regulatory speculation (C157-C159, C162-C163, C221-C223). Both rate as UNCERTAIN, noting plausible but unproven mechanisms. Partial overlap with aligned uncertainty.

Both address mechanistic speculation about BER pathway interactions (C164-C165 and broader claims C48-C49, C111-C113, C180-C184). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN noting speculation requires validation. Peer Reviewer 2 notes mechanisms are 'plausible' but need 'greater caution' until replicated. Strong concordance on uncertain/speculative status.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the evidence for Mbd4 as causal gene (C166-C173, C84, C124). OpenEval highlights conflicting evidence including mutation spectrum mismatch. Peer reviewers don't explicitly discuss Mbd4 but this contributes to overall uncertainty about gene identification. Aligned uncertainty.

Both support AMSD's superior performance compared to QTL mapping in the BXD context (C185-C192). OpenEval provides detailed mechanistic explanation for advantages, while peer reviewers affirm AMSD 'outperforms traditional QTL mapping' with greater power under specific conditions. Complete agreement.

Both support acknowledgment of AMSD limitations regarding relatedness modeling (C196-C197, C212-C214). OpenEval notes honest assessment of current capabilities, while peer reviewers explicitly note difficulty applying beyond recombinant inbred lines and accept balanced presentation of limitations. Agreement on limitations.

OpenEval R15 addresses the novel finding of epistasis between germline mutators in whole animals (C8-C10, C46-C49, C108-C113). Peer R4 strongly supports the epistasis finding with overlapping claims (C8-C10, C46-C47, C110). Both rate as SUPPORTED, though OpenEval notes mechanistic interpretation is speculative while peer review focuses on statistical evidence.

OpenEval R15 includes novelty claims about whole-animal epistasis (C111-C113) and mechanistic speculation (C48-C49), which peer R11 addresses as UNCERTAIN, noting mechanisms are plausible but need replication. Partial overlap with different emphasis: OpenEval supports epistasis finding while noting speculation; peer review emphasizes caution about mechanisms.

Peer R8 discusses Setmar as a candidate gene (C128-C135), noting reviewers accept authors' reasoning for excluding it as a strong candidate. No corresponding OpenEval result specifically addresses Setmar evaluation, though OpenEval discusses other candidate genes.

Peer R15 addresses broader applicability and significance of the AMSD method to other systems and populations (C200-C202, C205-C207, C210-C211, C215). No corresponding OpenEval result specifically evaluates these forward-looking applicability claims, though OpenEval discusses method performance in the BXD context.
